extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Mint/Burn Operations
extra_findings.description: The contract's Mint and Burn operations do not provide users with mechanisms to specify minimum acceptable outputs or execution bounds. When users request token minting or burning, they cannot protect themselves against unfavorable execution conditions. This exposes users to potential loss of funds if execution is incomplete or partial.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Issue in Mint Operations
extra_findings.description: The Mint operation validates parameters after state changes instead of before. The function executes the mint operation first, then validates parameters. This allows invalid operations to complete successfully, leading to protocol instability and potential fund loss.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Issue in Interface
extra_findings.description: The interface declares critical functions without access control indicators. Functions like pool creation, fee collection, parameter changes should indicate restrictions but do not. This is a vulnerability because interfaces should reflect security expectations for critical functions.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Issue in Function Chains
extra_findings.description: When functions call other internal functions, state is updated before the dependent call. This creates a synchronization issue where dependent functions may use stale state values, leading to incorrect calculations and potential fund loss.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Consistency Issue
extra_findings.description: When functions implement interfaces or override base functions, return values do not use expected units. This creates unit mismatches that cause incorrect calculations and accounting errors, potentially leading to fund loss.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions in the Cw721Query implementation lack mechanisms for users to specify acceptable execution bounds when managing approvals. This exposes users to unfavorable execution outcomes when approval states are modified, as they cannot protect against manipulation of approval states that affect their assets.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions validate approval states after loading token information from storage. This allows invalid approval states to be processed and returned to callers before validation occurs, potentially exposing users to manipulation of approval states that affect their assets.

extra_findings.title: Execution Boundaries and Validation Consistency Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions load token information from storage and then validate approval states. When execution differs from initial requests, these functions do not maintain consistency between expected and actual execution. The validation boundaries are not enforced at appropriate points relative to state changes, allowing invalid approval states to be processed.

extra_findings.title: Access Control Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions do not have access control modifiers. These functions are critical for managing approval states that affect user assets. Without access control, these functions can be called by anyone, potentially leading to manipulation of approval states that affect user assets.

extra_findings.title: State Synchronization Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions load token information from storage and then validate approval states. When execution differs from initial requests, these functions do not maintain consistency between expected and actual execution. The validation boundaries are not enforced at appropriate points relative to state changes, allowing invalid approval states to be processed.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Consistency Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions return approval information without ensuring the correct units. When callers use these approval values in calculations, unit mismatches cause incorrect calculations and accounting errors.

extra_findings.title: External System Assumptions Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions make assumptions about external system structure and behavior. These functions assume external system characteristics that could vary, leading to wrong parameter determination or logic errors.

extra_findings.title: Signature Execution Context Binding Issue in Approval Management Functions
extra_findings.description: The `owner_of`, `operator`, `operators`, `approval`, and `approvals` functions do not bind signature context to the intended executor/submitter address. This allows anyone can submit approval requests, potentially leading to manipulation of approval states that affect user assets.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Check in Operator Query Handler
extra_findings.description: The `operator` query handler in the Cw721Query implementation lacks verification that the caller is authorized to query operator information for the specified owner. This allows any user to query operator information for arbitrary addresses, potentially exposing sensitive access control information.

extra_findings.title: Critical: Missing User Protection in Withdraw Functions Allows Unauthorized Fund Extraction
extra_findings.description: The ExecuteMsg enum defines multiple Withdraw-related functions (Withdraw, WithdrawToLandlord) that allow fund extraction without user-specified minimum outputs or protective parameters. This violates Pattern 1 (Missing User Protection) and Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing) as funds can be withdrawn without user protection against manipulation or partial execution failures.

extra_findings.title: High: Validation Timing Vulnerability in Withdraw Functions Allows Invalid Operations to Complete
extra_findings.description: The Withdraw and WithdrawToLandlord functions likely validate parameters after state changes instead of before (Pattern 2). This allows invalid operations to complete, as validation occurs after token transfers, balance updates, or swap execution. Since validation timing is incorrect, invalid operations can complete, leading to fund loss.

extra_findings.title: High: Access Control Issues in ExecuteMsg Interface
extra_findings.description: The ExecuteMsg interface declares critical functions (Withdraw, WithdrawToLandlord) without access control indicators (Pattern 4). This is a vulnerability as interface design should reflect security expectations. Critical functions should indicate restrictions, but the interface shows no access control expectations for these functions.

extra_findings.title: High: State Synchronization Issues in Function Chains
extra_findings.description: The Withdraw and WithdrawToLandlord functions likely call other internal functions, and state may be updated before the dependent call (Pattern 6). This is a vulnerability as state modifications may happen before the dependent function executes. When operations reduce state values and trigger dependent operations, state may be set to final intended value before dependent function reads it. If dependent function reads state before reset, it may use stale state value.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State-Modifying Functions
extra_findings.description: The ContractError enum defines error types but no functions are visible in this file. However, since this is an error definition file, the vulnerability assessment must consider that if any functions in the broader contract (not shown) modify state variables used in economic calculations (e.g., deposits, rental amounts, approvals, balances), and those functions lack access control, users could manipulate timing or values before admin operations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Domain Validation in Mathematical Operations
extra_findings.description: The code lacks validation for mathematical domain constraints, particularly for logarithmic and square root operations. When invalid inputs (zero, negative values) are silently accepted, the operations produce mathematically impossible results without error.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Signature-Based Operations
extra_findings.description: The ContractError enum defines authorization-related errors like 'Ownership', 'ApprovedAlready', 'AlreadyReserved', 'NotApproved', 'NotListed', 'RentalActive', 'RentalAlreadyStarted', 'RentalNotActivated', 'UnavailablePeriod', 'InvalidInput', 'LessThanMinimum', 'Expired', 'RefundableAmount', and 'ApprovalNotFound'. However, none of these errors bind the authorization context (e.g., caller address, execution parameters) to the authorization signature or approval. This allows front-running attacks where an attacker can capture a valid authorization and replay it with hostile context (e.g., different recipient, amount, or parameters). The vulnerability is in the design of the error system itself, which lacks any authorization binding mechanism.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State-Modifying Functions
extra_findings.description: The file defines query message types but no actual query handler functions. However, the cw721 standard requires state management functions (e.g., transfer, approve, setApprovalForAll, etc.) are missing entirely. Without proper access control on state-modifying functions, any actor can manipulate token ownership, approvals, and operator permissions, leading to complete protocol compromise.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Withdrawal/Refund Operations
extra_findings.description: The ContractError enum defines a RefundableAmount error variant that includes an amount field: `RefundableAmount { amount: String }`. This indicates the contract has logic to calculate refundable amounts, but there is no corresponding function that implements the actual refund operation. Without a properly implemented refund function with user-controlled minimum acceptable output parameters, users cannot protect against manipulation of refund calculations.

extra_findings.title: Inconsistent State Management for Refund Calculations
extra_findings.description: The ContractError enum includes both `RefundableAmount { amount: String }` and `ApprovalNotFound { spender: String }` variants. This suggests the contract has logic to track refundable amounts and approval states, but there is no corresponding function that implements the actual refund operation. Without a properly implemented refund function with user-controlled minimum acceptable output parameters, users cannot protect against manipulation of refund calculations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Critical Operations
extra_findings.description: The ContractError enum includes `InsufficientDeposit {}`, `UnavailableAmount {}`, and `RefundableAmount { amount: String }` variants. This indicates the contract has logic to handle deposit amounts and refund calculations, but there is no corresponding function that implements the actual refund operation. Without a properly implemented refund function with user-controlled minimum acceptable output parameters, users cannot protect against manipulation of refund calculations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State-Modifying Functions in Query Module
extra_findings.description: The file cw721/src/query.rs defines numerous query-related data structures (e.g., Cw721QueryMsg variants, response structs like OwnerOfResponse, Approval, etc.), but it contains no functions that modify state. However, in a typical CW721 implementation, functions like `owner_of`, `approval`, `operator`, etc., would be implemented elsewhere (e.g., in execute.rs or contract.rs). If the corresponding execute functions (e.g., `update_owner`, `set_approval`, `remove_approval`, etc.) exist and modify state variables used in economic calculations (e.g., balances, deposits, fees, rental periods, cancellation terms), they must have proper access control. Without access control, attackers could manipulate state before admin operations, affecting fee calculations, deposit amounts, rental periods, and other economic parameters.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation in Query Messages
extra_findings.description: The Cw7221QueryMsg enum defines query messages but lacks validation for critical fields like token_id, owner, and spender addresses. This allows malformed inputs that could cause unexpected behavior in query execution.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Execute Traits Allows Unauthorized State Modification
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Execute trait defines multiple execute functions (transfer_nft, send_nft, approve, revoke, burn, etc.) without any access control modifiers. These functions modify critical state such as token ownership, approvals, and balances. Without access control, any actor can call these functions, enabling unauthorized transfers, approvals, and destruction of NFTs.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Cw721QueryMsg
extra_findings.description: The Cw721QueryMsg enum defines query messages for a CW721 (CosmWasm NFT) implementation, but lacks any authorization context binding. This means that any actor can construct valid query messages for arbitrary token IDs and owner addresses without cryptographic binding to the intended requester. This enables front-running attacks where malicious actors can construct queries that appear legitimate but are actually unauthorized access attempts.

extra_findings.title: Type Representation Ambiguity in Cw721QueryMsg Fields
extra_findings.description: The Cw721QueryMsg enum defines fields like token_id: String, owner: String, spender: String, etc. These are defined as generic String types without explicit validation or normalization. In CosmWasm/CW721 implementations, token IDs are typically expected to be non-empty strings, but the type system does not enforce this. This creates ambiguity in value representation - the same logical token ID could be represented as different string values (e.g., 'token123' vs ' token123' with leading space) that would compare equal semantically but have different bit representations. If equality operations compare raw string bytes without normalization, these equivalent values would compare as unequal.

extra_findings.title: Missing State Commitment Timing for Query Operations
extra_findings.description: The Cw721QueryMsg enum defines multiple query operations (OwnerOf, Approval, Approvals, Operator, etc.) but lacks explicit state commitment timing semantics. In CosmWasm, query operations should be idempotent and not modify state, but the current definition doesn't prevent stateful implementations. If a query operation modifies state (e.g., increments counters, logs access), and the state is committed before operation verification, this creates a timing vulnerability. An attacker could craft queries that appear to succeed but leave state in an inconsistent condition.

extra_findings.title: Missing Interface Definition Compatibility for External Protocol Integration
extra_findings.description: The Cw721QueryMsg enum defines query messages for a CW721 (CosmWasm NFT) implementation, but lacks explicit interface definition compatibility with external protocols. The enum defines query operations but doesn't specify parameter counts, struct field completeness, or function name compatibility with external NFT protocols. This creates ABI encoding mismatches when integrating with external NFT protocols. For example, if the external protocol expects 6 parameters but the interface declares 5, or if the Route struct is missing required fields like factory address, encoding/decoding fails.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Query Functions
extra_findings.description: The query functions in this file (OwnerOf, Approval, Approvals, Operator, AllOperators, Tokens, AllTokens) do not provide users with mechanisms to specify acceptable execution bounds or minimum acceptable outputs. While these are query functions (view calls), the lack of user control parameters means users cannot express their acceptable outcomes, making them vulnerable to MEV extraction or front-running attacks where malicious actors can manipulate the execution environment to extract value from users.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Critical Execute Functions in Cw721Execute Interface
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Execute trait defines 10 critical execute functions (transfer_nft, send_nft, approve, revoke, approve_all, revoke_all, burn) but provides no access control mechanisms. These functions modify state, transfer assets, or change permissions without any access restrictions. In the context of a CW721 (CosmWasm NFT standard), these functions are typically only meant to be callable by the NFT owner or authorized operators, but the interface provides no way to enforce this. This is a critical vulnerability because it allows any actor to perform these operations on any NFT, leading to complete loss of asset control.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization in Cw721Execute Trait Methods
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Execute trait defines execute methods (transfer_nft, send_nft, approve, etc.) but lacks explicit authorization checks in the trait definition. Implementations must verify caller authorization before executing state-changing operations. Without proper authorization, any caller could execute privileged operations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization in Cw721Query Trait Methods
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Query trait defines query methods (owner_of, operator, approvals, etc.) but lacks explicit authorization checks in the trait definition. While query methods typically don't change state, some implementations may perform state changes in query methods (e.g., for gas refunds, rebates). Without authorization checks, attackers could trigger unauthorized state changes through query methods.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Signature-Based Operations
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Execute trait defines multiple authorization-sensitive operations (transfer_nft, send_nft, burn, approve, revoke, approve_all, revoke_all) but provides no mechanism to bind the intended executor or execution context to the authorization. This allows front-runners to submit operations with hostile contexts, consuming nonces/signatures before the intended user can execute.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Call Function
extra_findings.description: The `call` function in `Cw721Contract` executes arbitrary messages without allowing users to specify minimum acceptable outputs or execution bounds. This exposes users to unfavorable execution outcomes when operations can be partially completed or manipulated.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Issue in Call Function
extra_findings.description: The `call` function executes WasmMsg::Execute without validating the message content before execution. If the message is malformed or invalid, the execution could complete with invalid state changes before any validation occurs.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control in Interface
extra_findings.description: The `Cw721Contract` interface declares critical functions like `call` without access control indicators. Functions that execute arbitrary messages should indicate restrictions but none are present in the interface declaration.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Mismatch in tokens Function
extra_findings.description: The `tokens` function returns `StdResult<TokensResponse>` but the caller may expect a different unit structure. When the caller uses this return value in calculations, the unit mismatch causes incorrect accounting.

extra_findings.title: Return Value Unit Mismatch in all_tokens Function
extra_findings.description: The `all_tokens` function returns `StdResult<TokensResponse>` but the caller may expect a different unit structure. When the caller uses this return value in calculations, the unit mismatch causes incorrect accounting.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on `call` Function Allows Unauthorized Contract Interaction
extra_findings.description: The `call` function in the `Cw721Contract` struct performs a critical operation: it executes messages to a CW721 contract. This function has no access control restrictions, allowing any entity to invoke it. Since this function directly interacts with external contracts and can trigger state changes, it requires access control to prevent unauthorized operations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Caller Verification in Automatic Handlers
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Contract helper struct provides query and execution methods but lacks any caller verification in its call() method. While this file itself doesn't contain automatic currency handlers, the vulnerability pattern emerges when this contract is used in broader context where the contract receives native tokens without verification.

extra_findings.title: Authorization Context Binding Missing in Signature Verification
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Contract implementation lacks proper binding of authorization context (executor, parameters) in signature verification. The `call` method accepts any `ExecuteMsg<T, E>` without verifying that the caller is authorized or that the message parameters match the intended authorization. This allows front-running attacks where an attacker can intercept an authorization and submit it with hostile parameters.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on NFT Minting and State Initialization Functions
extra_findings.description: The trait interface defines multiple execute functions (e.g., `transfer_nft`, `send_nft`, `approve`, `revoke`, `approve_all`, `revoke_all`, `burn`) but lacks any access control on state-modifying operations. In particular, functions that initialize or update critical economic state (e.g., ownership, approvals, rental terms, token existence) are publicly callable without authorization, enabling front-running, state manipulation, and fee avoidance.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Approve/ApproveAll Functions Enables Allowance Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The Cw721ExecuteMsg enum defines Approve and ApproveAll operations, but the file contains only the message definition, not the implementation. However, in typical cw721 implementations, these functions update state (allowance mappings) that are used in economic calculations (e.g., transfer permissions, fees, rewards). Without proper access control (e.g., `only_owner` or `can_approve` checks), any user can manipulate these allowances at critical times.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Check in ApproveAll and Approve Operations
extra_findings.description: The Cw721ExecuteMsg enum defines Approve and ApproveAll operations that allow operators to manage tokens on behalf of owners. However, the message definition itself does not include any authorization verification. In a secure implementation, these operations should verify that the caller is either the token owner or an authorized operator. Without this check, any actor could approve themselves or others to manage tokens, leading to unauthorized token transfers.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Approve/ApproveAll Messages
extra_findings.description: The Cw721ExecuteMsg enum defines Approve and ApproveAll messages that allow operators to manage allowances, but these messages lack binding of the token owner's address in the authorization context. This allows front-running attacks where an attacker can submit the same authorization with a different token ID or spender, consuming the allowance without the owner's intent.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on `into_cosmos_msg` Allows Unauthorized Message Construction
extra_findings.description: The `into_cosmos_msg` method in `Cw721ReceiveMsg` constructs a `WasmMsg::Execute` without verifying the caller's authorization. Since this function is public and not restricted by any access control modifiers, any external actor can construct arbitrary `Execute` messages targeting any contract address. This enables attackers to construct malicious messages that could be used in replay attacks, front-running, or to bypass intended receiver-side validation logic.

extra_findings.title: Missing Input Validation on `token_id` and `sender` Fields Enables Invalid Message Construction
extra_findings.description: The `Cw721ReceiveMsg` struct accepts `sender: String` and `token_id: String` fields without validation. Since `into_cosmos_msg` directly serializes these fields into a `WasmMsg::Execute`, an attacker can construct messages with invalid addresses (e.g., malformed Bech32 strings, empty strings, or excessively long strings). This can cause downstream receivers to revert unexpectedly or behave incorrectly when processing these messages. The lack of validation also enables denial-of-service via message bloat or injection attacks.

extra_findings.title: Missing Error Handling on `into_binary` Failure Leaves Message Construction Incomplete
extra_findings.description: The `into_cosmos_msg` function calls `self.into_binary()?`, which may fail if serialization fails. However, the function does not handle this failure explicitly, and the `?` operator propagates the error. While this prevents message construction on failure, it does not provide context about why the failure occurred. More critically, if `into_binary` fails after partial state mutation (e.g., if this were a stateful operation), the caller would receive an error but no message, leaving the operation in an ambiguous state. In a stateful context, this could lead to inconsistent accounting if the caller assumes the message was constructed successfully.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Cw721Receiver Interface
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Receiver interface declares the receive_nft function without any access control restrictions. This allows any external actor to invoke the function and manipulate state or trigger logic that should be restricted to authorized entities.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on State-Modifying Functions in Cw721Contract
extra_findings.description: The Cw721Contract struct implements several functions that query external state but lack access control. While the provided code shows only query functions, the pattern reveals a critical access control boundary violation: functions that read and return state used in economic calculations (e.g., token balances, operator approvals, ownership) are publicly callable without any access restrictions. This enables front-running, MEV extraction, and timing-based manipulation of state-dependent operations.

extra_findings.title: Missing Receiver Implementation for CW721 NFT Receiver Pattern
extra_findings.description: The provided code defines data structures for CW721 NFT receive messages but does not implement the required CW721 receiver interface. This means contracts attempting to receive CW721 tokens will not properly handle incoming tokens, potentially causing permanent token loss.

extra_findings.title: Missing Authorization Context Binding in Cw721ReceiverMsg
extra_findings.description: The Cw721ReceiveMsg struct lacks binding of the intended recipient address in its serialization. This allows any actor can forge receive messages for arbitrary token IDs and senders, bypassing the Cw721 standard's authorization requirements.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Mint Function
extra_findings.description: The contract's Mint function lacks access control, allowing any user to mint new tokens without authorization. This is a critical vulnerability as it enables unlimited token inflation and potential token devaluation.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Approve/ApproveAll Functions
extra_findings.description: The Approve and ApproveAll functions allow operators to transfer or spend tokens on behalf of the owner without requiring the owner to specify minimum acceptable outputs or execution bounds. This exposes owners to unfavorable execution where operators could transfer more value than intended or at inopportune times.

extra_findings.title: Missing User Protection in Transfer Function
extra_findings.description: The TransferNft function does not provide users with mechanisms to specify minimum acceptable outputs or execution bounds. When users request token transfers, they cannot protect against unfavorable execution conditions, exposing them to potential loss of value due to market manipulation or adversarial actions.

extra_findings.title: Validation Timing Issue in Mint Function
extra_findings.description: The Mint function executes token creation before validating that the token ID is unique and the minter has sufficient authority. This allows invalid operations to complete, potentially leading to token inflation or unauthorized minting.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control on Mint Function Enables Fee Evasion via Timing Manipulation
extra_findings.description: The contract's Mint function lacks access control, allowing any user to mint tokens at arbitrary times. This enables front-running of admin operations and manipulation of state used in economic calculations. Specifically, if the contract implements fee calculations based on time of day, block timestamps, or other time-dependent variables, users can time their mint operations to avoid fees or gain unfair advantages.

extra_findings.title: Missing Access Control in Minter Management
extra_findings.description: The contract implements a CW721 NFT minter pattern but lacks proper access control on minter management functions. The `Minter` query response shows the minter is set to admin, but there's no verification that only the minter can mint tokens. An attacker could potentially call mint functions directly if the minter address is compromised or if the minter is set to a predictable address.
